tagline: Farmland roads link old mill communities and a colonial meetinghouse
intro: The Upper Freehold Historic Farmland Scenic Byway links Allentown with farmland and mill communities in Monmouth County. The drive follows county and local roads, including Rues Road and Red Valley Road. New Jersey DOT identifies history and culture as the scenic byway’s defining qualities and describes a corridor where agricultural traditions remain visible. Its published length is approximately 24 miles. Allentown and Imlaystown are historic districts within the corridor, and the neighboring farms have been here for multiple generations.

The roads connect settlements shaped by farming and milling. At Walnford, Philadelphia merchant Richard Waln bought several mills in 1772 and built a house the following year. The road network changed: two sections of Walnford Road that once joined now require a circuit through other roads to reach the mill.

Following DOT’s detailed tour, begin at Allentown’s Presbyterian Church and head out along Main Street toward Chambers Road and Rues Road. Route 526 leads toward Red Valley Road, with a northward spur to the Old Yellow Meeting House. Continue by Holmes Mill Road and Arneytown-Hornerstown Road to Hill Road, then cross Crosswicks Creek on the old iron bridge. The final approach ends at Walnford Mill. An optional return from the mill takes drivers back through Holmes Mill Road toward Allentown.

moments.title: Imlaystown
moments.text: A 28-acre millpond served two businesses in Imlaystown: milling and ice. The community dates to 1690 and takes its name from the Imlay family, major colonial landowners. Much of the town was rebuilt in 1898 after a destructive fire. Salter’s Mill also replaced an earlier mill damaged by fire, and its two-and-a-half-story frame building contains a horizontal turbine wheel. The Golden family closed milling operations in 1962; the millpond was restored in 1995. The historic district also includes a two-story brick school built in 1930 in the Colonial Revival style.
moments.notice: Salter’s Mill stands beside the 28-acre millpond.

moments.title: Old Yellow Meeting House
moments.text: The meetinghouse’s gable ends face east and west, an arrangement intended to maximize sunlight on its southern side. An earlier Baptist meeting building went up in 1720 on land Thomas and Rachel Salter donated. The present meetinghouse followed in 1737. The cemetery preserves an earlier date: its oldest dated grave belongs to their son John, who died on August 29, 1723. The byway’s spur reaches the meetinghouse north of Route 526 on Yellow Meeting House Road. The congregation’s first resident minister was David Jones; the meetinghouse is the oldest Baptist meetinghouse in New Jersey.
moments.notice: The gable ends face east and west.

moments.title: Walnford
moments.text: Walnford’s gristmill stands on Crosswicks Creek, within a historic district that also includes Richard Waln’s 1773 house. Waln was a Philadelphia merchant who bought several mills here in 1772 and gave the settlement its name. His son Nicolas inherited the property, and descendants lived here for nearly 200 years. The preserved complex includes a carriage house and cow barn as well as the restored Georgian house and mill. The district entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1976 for its significance in agriculture and commerce. Walnford Road ends at the mill.
moments.notice: The gristmill sits on Crosswicks Creek; the historic district also includes Waln’s 1773 house.
